name: Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes
aliases: Adaptive GPU Workload Distribution, Flexible Workload Distribution
text:
# Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes

Also called: Adaptive GPU Workload Distribution, Flexible Workload Distribution

## Overview
Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes are methods that distribute rendering workload between a fast GPU (performing raycasting or image warping) and a slow GPU (performing raycasting) to improve visual quality beyond strict node assignment by replacing some image warping with raycasting [S1]. Unlike separation planes which create perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading approximation and poor adaptation to scene interest, flexible schemes adapt to focus [regions, segmentations](#9712-region-growing-segmentation.md), or depth importance [S1].

## Shared principles
The core principle is the relaxation of strict workload assignment between fast and slow nodes. When viewport resolution and sampling rate are small enough, raycasting on modern GPUs can be acceptably fast, allowing visual quality to be improved by replacing some of the image warping with raycasting [S1]. This approach requires special attention to the amount of workload shifted, as it reduces the frame rate of the fast node [S1]. The latency compensation step of the system is extended by raycasting to handle these dynamic assignments [S1].

## Subtopics

### Distribution by Quality Maps
Distribution by Quality Maps is a workload distribution method that uses a quality map to identify badly reconstructed pixels (mostly from disocclusions or undersampling during image warping) and replaces them with high-quality raycasting [S1].

**Step:**
On the fast node:
1. Use image warping to reconstruct $m$ layers.
2. Project the volume’s bounding geometry to the screen.
3. Iterate through the closest $m$ layers for each pixel covered by the projection.
4. If layers are empty, raycast this pixel.

**Parameter:**
$m$: The number of empty layers required per pixel to classify the pixel as disoccluded. A lower $m$ switches to raycasting more frequently [S1].

**Pitfall:**
In [layered image warping](#11344-layered-image-warping.md), completely empty pixels are rare, but holes in foremost layers commonly happen and disocclude content from back layers, resulting in unsatisfying reconstructions. The parameter $m$ helps steer the quality vs. performance tradeoff [S1].

**Comparison:**
Performance scales with frame-to-frame coherence: large viewpoint motion induces more raycasting (lower performance), while slow motion allows more warped fragments. Unlike fixed layer counts, this is user-input dependent [S1].

## Background
Origin: S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg, "[Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering](#11326-multi-frame-rate-volume-rendering.md)" (2010) [S1]. The method addresses the limitations of traditional parallel raycasting algorithms that divide workload by separation planes in screen space or object space (sort-first or sort-last), which often lead to perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading from warped images being only an approximation to per-sample [phong shading](#1853-phong-shading.md) [S1]. These regions do not adapt well to what is really interesting in a scene, such as focus regions, segmentations, or magic lenses [S1]. The authors propose a more flexible workload distribution to account for the fact that features close to the current viewpoint are more important and better perceivable than distant features [S1].
